title: No Bad Memories
summary: Robbie Chater, Tony Di Blasi and Andy Szekeres discuss No Bad Memories, sampling and forgotten technologies. They reflect on the connections between advertising, childhood and memory, and following instinct while making their new record.
transcript:
Robbie Chater, Tony Di Blasi and Andy Szekeres of The Avalanches join Lauren Taylor on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, to discuss No Bad Memories, 15 October 2026.

At the very top there we heard a rare 70s soul track that was recorded by the late American soul singer Wilson Williams. I Can't Get Used to Losing You was the name of the track that the Avalanches sampled on their latest record. The track Can't Get Over Losing You featuring Portraits of Tracy. We followed it up with some Avalanches and such a great reinterpretation of Since I Left You that was produced around the early 2000s but was officially part of a wider release on the Avalanches Since I Left You, the 20th anniversary deluxe edition a few years ago. The Stereolab remix of Since I Left You and pretty special to hear the Avalanches dropping the original of that track in the RRR performance space to close their set recently if you were in the room for that. Very special moment.

We also heard the track Blue Shadows featuring of course Karen O from Yeah Yeah Yeahs, sampling a Balearic classic from Blue Gas. Karen O, just one of the many collaborators on the new Avalanches album. Their fourth record, and their first in six years, No Bad Memories, which comes out tomorrow. And we're about to jump into an extended interview with The Avalanches, who need no introduction, but they are indeed Melbourne electronic royalty. Since the release of their iconic debut album Since I Left You, the group have really helped to lay the foundations for sample-driven music in the 21st century to become really one of the most influential Australian acts of all time. The line-up has changed for the Avalanches over the years since the band formed back in 1997 and they now exist as a trio in the current configuration. Two original members, Robbie Chater and Tony Di Blasi, joined by regular collaborator Andy Szekeres of Midnight Juggernauts fame.

I guess experimenting with sound and memory and nostalgia has really always been at the heart of what the Avalanches do. And on this latest album, the sounds of advertising and technology were really calling to the band. The album artwork that you're probably familiar with sees a floppy disk and an iPod as characters holding hands. I thought of them as mascots for the emotional core of this new record, with the band describing their new album as an ode to the ways corporate advertising and commercial jingles wrapped themselves around our childhoods. The Avalanches, of course, a group famous for digging through obscure vinyl crates, but for their latest album, they dove headfirst into digging for old start-up sounds and audio logos. The first single they released from the album, Together, with Nikki Nair sort of famously samples the start-up sound from Nokia. The album campaign as well... Not only did the band create a text-based alternate reality game around a mysterious fictional entity called Takumi Digital Archives, but for the very first time, an Avalanches album is also set to be accompanied by a film, blending live action, collage, animation and other various things that Robbie Chater co-directed with long-time collaborator and artist Jonathan Zawada, which is due for release next year.

And as I mentioned, the Avalanches dropped by RRR recently during Radiothon, of course, for that very special live DJ set in the RRR performance space. They played an exclusive set for RRR subscribers to help celebrate our 50th birthday. Perhaps you were one of the lucky ones in the room that night. It was very, very fun. And I was very fortunate to get to host that event and also to chat to the band in studio before they hit the stage, where together we went really deep into the world of No Bad Memories. And here's how it went down with Robbie, Tony and Andy from the Avalanches when they joined me in the studio.

Welcome Robbie and Tony and Andy as well. The official third member now of the Avalanches, I guess marking the first time the Avalanches have operated as a three piece in like a decade now. Maybe to start with you, you've had a long history with the band sort of coming up as musical contemporaries with Midnight Juggernauts. You played bass on the Wildflower tour as well, is that right?

I think there was a bit of recorded stuff, I think, in the pre-production sort of stuff. I didn't actually perform, not live performing.

I completely forgot about that. Yeah.

You did too. That's a good note that you've got there because I would have forgotten that too.

But yeah, in terms of... That was, I guess, technically the beginning of doing any kind of work with the guys. But mainly it really got started as a testing out, doing some writing and recording in the lead up to We Will Always Love You. So, which is probably... I don't know how many years ago that was, but it would have been the beginning of the writing of that album. And I guess it's just sort of organically grown from there to now.

And you've been heavily involved, I guess, with shaping the new album. It's sort of a thematic concept as well. The track Blue Shadows featuring Karen O, I understand, was an idea of yours that was almost lost to time. Is that right? Can you tell us that story?

Yeah, I suppose that was a, yeah, one of the tracks on this record that's one of the earliest sort of ideas, I would say.

Would that be fair to say? Like in terms of like in the writing process?

I think it was almost, maybe there was, I can't remember what it was. I think it was during the... I remember trying to find it, re-find it. Yeah, I think during the writing of We Will Always Love You, it may have been, it definitely didn't have Karen O, but I think it was an idea from that time.

How did it get overlooked?

Maybe it was waiting for Karen O to do something with it. So, yeah, waiting for Karen.

And you discovered it, Tony?

I think so, yeah. I remember. There's so much stuff floating around, you just kind of go through all the old archives and depending on the time in your life, like things just jump out at you differently.

That's so true. It's like, because you could, yeah, you're just in a different headspace and sometimes you miss really great things, I think, depending on what you're looking for.

I guess, yeah, Andy, you've transitioned now from a collaborator to like an official third member. Yeah, did Robbie and Tony give you any sort of official like initiation or did it just sort of feel like a natural evolution?

We wanted to do it.

Have you seen the Some Kind of Monster documentary? When Metallica get the new bass player.

I'm still waiting for that moment, actually.

So they offer him a million dollars. So we wanted to do that.

[Unclear audio at 00:07:14–00:07:18]

And Robbie and Tony, you've openly said that you don't sort of talk in technical terms to each other. You've got this unspoken language that's built entirely on feeling and you never thought you'd meet anyone else who spoke to you that way until Andy came along. What was the moment you realised, you know, Andy's sort of not helping us out anymore... You're going to make him an official member of the Avalanches?

I'm not sure. I guess because it has been a long time now, it just became that way. I don't know.

Yeah, I think there was a time where it was like, oh, let's get him in officially. I think it was just organically. We were like, oh, this guy keeps hanging around. You may as well let him in. All right, boy, you keep coming.

Well, you know, it was like I was thinking earlier, because it's like it's quite labour intensive work. And we all work alone in separate states, actually, the last few years. And, you know, just the nature of sampling, it's long hours. And so it's really lovely to have that friendship with two other people that do what you do. And then it's just a lovely sort of everlasting, ever-growing text chain. And then at a certain point, you sort of start to say, morning, mates. And we're all saying good morning. And good night. And then you say good night, which we do every night. I was just reflecting before, it's like it's a really sweet and lovely thing. So I guess it's like, I don't know, it's like any relationship, all of a sudden you're just like saying good night.

He's moved his toothbrush in.

Exactly.

Well, congratulations on the new record, the fourth album, the first in six years for the Avalanches, No Bad Memories. Being four albums deep, I guess now, there's kind of a common theme with all your records, this feeling of motion. Since I Left You, you know, initially it was titled Pablo's Cruise, this kind of imaginary journey around the world. Wildflower was this dreamy soundtrack to a road trip on LSD. With We Will Always Love You, you know, these voices become transmissions that are beaming into space. Is No Bad Memories a journey back in time? Or where does it take you?

Yeah, it's a good question. I'm not sure so much if it makes me think of a physical, like a physical location. But I think it is, well, as with all our records, exploring memory and our sense of self and what makes us, I guess. A big part of it was reflecting on growing up in this, I guess, capitalist world and how all the advertising and everything we consume growing up shapes us. That's kind of where we... That was the jumping-off point, I think.

Take us into the world of No Bad Memories. Like, why did those themes sort of come up as ones that you felt compelled to explore on this new record?

I think it began with, we were looking at a lot of the devices that we used to store our memories when, like, when we were younger from, you know, CDs to iPods to, I'm trying to think, making, you know, mixtapes for each other or, you know, old video cameras. And then we just began looking more and more at the advertising around those products and that was like a whole other rabbit hole that we really enjoyed going down and the incredible art and music that was associated with the advertising of those items.

Your relationship to technology. I guess The Avalanches have this incredible way of making, you know, forgotten machines sound human and turning discarded technology into something that's really joyful. I wanted to wind back to the making of Wildflower, because I don't understand, Robbie. It was important for you to use the same equipment that you made Since I Left You with. I think a program called Studio Vision that they stopped making the software for back in 1998. There's legendary stories of you having to, like, lug an old 30 kilogram beige Mac computer from studio to studio, sort of wrapped in towels and blankets.

We kept kind of going, hey, if we move everything somewhere else, we'll be able to finish it. And then we kind of go there and then it wouldn't finish. And then we'd be lugging around in the back of the van.

You had a ute at one point?

I had many different cars during the 16 years.

I remember I can picture that monitor wrapped in, like, a blanket in the back of a ute going down to Point Lonsdale.

That's right. And we always had these fantasies about when it was done, we were going to throw it off a bridge and just watch it explode. I think it just got put out, like, with hard rubbish, though, so it wasn't quite as romantic.

Oh, so The Avalanches have finally let go of the blankets and the beige Mac. It's no more.

Yeah.

I guess in terms of the ways you're transforming forgotten technologies on this new record, you've noted the familiar whirring and coughing of an external hard drive coming to life. Why did that sound become a particular favourite for you?

Oh, for me, that's actually very nostalgic. Just those old big three and a half, oh, no, the five-inch floppy drives that you'd do, like, projects on at school and stuff. But making, Since I Left You in particular, because the Akai samplers we used, every sound was saved on a floppy disk. And I just remember that coughing.

Oh, that is, yeah.

It's just seared into my brain, so it's a very sort of nostalgic sound.

When we used to play live, we could just put one song on a floppy disk, so we'd just have to load after every song and stop. And then there's like 30 seconds of just silence while you're waiting for [Unclear audio at 00:12:30–00:12:42]. I ended up praying that it would load.

I guess, yeah, those old hard drives you used to store your personal memories on, sort of eventually becoming the literal, like, building blocks for your new music and making new memories. There's a beautiful, like, loop there. When you dig into those forgotten technologies, do you feel like you're kind of excavating your past in a way, or trying to tap into the memory that sort of lives inside these old machines, or is that a bit conceptual?

No, definitely, definitely, it's...

You're really getting on our level, aren't you?

Yeah, you should join the band, too.

No, it's, like, it's just so evocative, and even, like, we began reflecting on jingles and how catchy they are and how they can stay with you for decades as well, whether it's for a series or whatever from your childhood, and then you'll hear it all those years later, and it's so... That can take you back to a time and a place as well. It's so powerful, that stuff. And it was interesting exploring that, where that line is between, you know, what's our choice of memories and what's the stuff that's sort of been fed to us and to sell products and how, you know, it's like something can be really nostalgic and familiar, but it was also, I guess, yeah, just marketing in a way.

I guess, yeah, sort of sound and nostalgia have always been at the heart of what the Avalanches do. Does, you know, when you're sampling, like, a start-up sound from a commercial jingle, does it feel different than sampling, like, an old, obscure soul record? Do you feel like you're liberating these sounds from their corporate frameworks or something?

Actually, in that way...

[Unclear audio at 00:14:13–00:14:16]

Yeah, it does, it does, yeah. In that way, it does, actually.

But we didn't sample any ads.

No, we didn't.

No, we didn't.

Right, okay. I guess as masters of sampling, what do you think is, like, the secret formula that makes those kind of corporate jingles stick in your brain for decades? Do you think there's a formula?

It was interesting because we began writing our own, too, and went down a whole other path that took quite some time. And a few of those moments have made the album, but I've been inventing our own products and writing all the jingles for them, which was kind of a really fun and inspiring part of the project.

I don't know, Andy, what do you reckon?

Yeah, I mean, that was definitely... I do remember, when the concept of the record was really taking shape, there was a good three or four months of YouTubing all sorts of advertising jingles and watching intro logos for film companies and just listening to so much amazing music. And so much of it, yeah, is sort of stuck there, and it is a sort of strange rabbit hole to go down as well, because it's sort of like, I don't know. It's very technology-specific, too, of those certain things from those eras and those sort of glistening, I don't know, DX7s. Yeah, and it's weird, like, ending up in places like learning how the start-up sound for the first PlayStation was made, and there's all these elaborate stories behind the making of these, and then you realise you're really stuck somewhere when you're doing that. But kind of amazing, because, I mean, behind all that stuff, even though there is this side of it that's all about selling a product, then these amazing creative people have had careers, you know, writing their own original music, but then doing all this corporate work. And there are strange things to put together and how you feel about that.

Yeah, there's real artistry involved in the filming of them and the making of them, and that's the thing. It is meant to, like, get in your head and stay there and hypnotise you into buying that product.

How did you sort of balance that? I guess, yeah, The Avalanches have sort of always had this emotional sweet spot between the happy and sad, and the title, No Bad Memories sounds, you know, positive on the surface, but, yeah, as you're saying, there's sort of this insidious nostalgia of modern marketing. How do you balance the joy of the music with, like, the sadder reality of how the memories were formed, I guess?

It's, I think, I'm not sure, I think we actually set out to just, to make a record that wasn't conceptual at all. It's all sounding just so complex...

How's your brain going, though?

I'm really struggling to keep up.

He's like, I thought we were finished.

I thought the record was done, and I didn't have to keep...

It's only just begun, I think.

We were talking about that, though, like, today, about you still want to put this record on and just listen to it without any of the stuff attached to it and go, gee, this is a great record. I love the way this sounds. But there's obviously so many other layers to it that, yeah, I mean, I think makes it more special because there's these other things. But hopefully you can listen to it without all that stuff and just...

Yeah.

Yeah, people... You still can't listen to it without knowing all the stuff. Maybe some of it will be confusing to you without the concept. I know it sounds really confusing at the moment. But it'll be fine. Just put it on.

I remember so clearly after we finished the last album, because Tone and I were a bit scarred after that 16-year journey of making Wildflower. And then it was such a joy to work with Andy on We Will Always Love You, which was relatively quick. But it still was quite deep conceptually. And after it was finished, I remember Tone just being like, no more concepts, no more themes, no more.

I think we were talking party.

And it was like, just a happy party record. You put it on, everyone dancing. Eight tracks.

Yeah.

Yeah.

And yet here we are again.

Hey, guys, have you seen that Tame Impala just put out a record going 35 minutes?

Let's do that.

There's a track from it called Far Away featuring John Glacier and Khadija Al Hanafi.

[Unclear audio at 00:18:42–00:20:50]

And you also heard a little pop and pour audio ID from synth pioneer Suzanne Ciani. A little sonic reference that I thought I'd just pop in there for you as it does come up in the next section of the interview. The Avalanches have assembled a pretty extraordinary cast of collaborators on this new album, of which Suzanne is one of them. But also Karen O, who we heard from earlier, Jamie xx, Nikki Nair, Panda Bear, John Glacier, who we played for you just then, Mike Patton, and even actor Haley Joel Osment, who is perhaps best known to many as the child actor from Forrest Gump and The Sixth Sense.

One of the many collaborators on your new album is synth pioneer Suzanne Ciani, who I guess really helped to define the sonic language of modern advertising through her pioneering work creating audio identities for companies like Coca-Cola and Atari. The theme music to this program, Breaking and Entering, is actually an old little ID that she made for like a, what was it, an ITV commercial, I think, yeah, back in the day. Can you tell us about working with Suzanne and what her work means to you?

Suzanne is absolutely incredible and incredibly inspiring and there's like unbelievable YouTube videos of her. I think there's a Sesame Street one, teaching kids about a synthesizer and I think there's incredible ones of her on Letterman as well. But there's albums of hers, of her own synth work, but then there's compilations of her work doing the corporate tags and they're just absolutely remarkable. And so we spoke to her about making some new music years ago and that never happened. And then on this album, her speaking voice is actually phenomenal. So we've stitched together samples of her voice from different interviews and then recontacted her and asked if we could have permission to use her voice for that stuff, which is a lovely sort of full circle because her work in the corporate world had been so inspiring. Like there's one particular logo she does for Coca-Cola where she recreates the sound of Coke bottle popping and the pouring sound and the fizzing and it's all done with modular synthesizers and it's just, it's crazy.

Didn't we have a sample and we had to take it off for some reason of the pop and pour?

Yeah, yeah, yeah.

Sorry, just reminiscing there.

The album also sees you working with Panda Bear, Noah Lennox for the first time and yeah, along with Jamie xx, who you've reunited with on this record. His record In Colour and the Panda Bear album Person Pitch you've cited as helping you fall in love with sampling again. What was it finally like bringing Noah into The Avalanches' sonic world?

A few people have actually said to me, oh, I thought you've worked with him.

I thought that too, to be honest.

Yeah, and I think it just sort of feels like that because there's just, I guess there's a parallel with his sampling and they both, both projects can have that sort of lysergic, dreamy, summery, shimmery sort of feel and I remember when Person Pitch came out and we were still lost in the Wildflower wilderness and that was a really inspiring record for us.

That's such a beautiful record. And it feels very avalanches-y as well.

It does, yeah, I really connected with that music and yeah, so it was lovely to finally work together.

There's obviously so many collaborators on this new album, too many to go through individually today, but I did want to ask about one in particular, which is Haley Joel Osment. How the hell does he end up on an avalanches record?

I don't, well... We were speaking the other day and because...

He's saying the same thing actually. He's saying the same thing because I was saying...

I think he literally wrote that on his Instagram just recently.

He did, yeah.

Because we've made a film that's also called No Bad Memories that's going to be coming out next year, that we made with our friend Jonathan Zawada and Haley. And so we were meant to be just doing that, and then somehow he's ended up on... He just became such a good friend, and he's a big fan of the band. And we just kind of got him to do some voiceover stuff, and he's got a remarkable voice, and he does, like, some anime stuff or things like that. So yeah, it was amazing working with him and actually getting him on an album and as an Avalanches fan being on a record. Yeah, it's been very funny.

Actually, the longer... Because we were driving around rural Japan in the snow for weeks, and just, like, you really sort of... His sense of... Because we were self-producing this film, so it wasn't like a high-budget thing. So his sense of humour really sort of kept it all together and kept everybody positive each day when we were, like, shivering in the snow. And after a couple of weeks, we were like... We just realised he's such a funny guy, and his voice is so unbelievable, and he so embraced the themes of the film and the album that he just ended up...

He was always riffing on the El Dorado cola and all those... It's kind of teasing us and making fun of all that.

Yeah, I think he was auditioning during that.

On your last record you mentioned you sent notes to each of the collaborators to make sure that everyone sort of understood where you were coming from and your intentions. Did you work the same way again with this new record?

Maybe a little and I think some of the people like Karen we've worked with before and Rivers so that was sort of simpler. But I think people...

Well, we were lucky because we had sort of the film project and some... Like a script and stuff. If people were curious, we could send them that stuff, and that sort of explained it very well. And then with someone like Mike Patton, he's just so immersed in the world of gaming consoles and that kind of thing anyway. That's, like, his passion. So as soon as we mentioned that era of Sega, that sort of bro-y frat-boy Sega...

Bullying you into buying it. It's like, you idiot! Buy this product!

Yeah, like he sort of knew exactly where you were coming from. So, yeah.

Incredible. Well, I won't keep you too long because I know that you're incredibly jet-lagged, but I did want to just finally ask you... I think when we last spoke to you with Simon in 2020, around the release of We Will Always Love You, you spoke about a mantra that you had when you were writing that record, like, writing it from the heart, record it from the heart, follow the heart. Was there something that became the mantra for this new record? No Bad Memories?

I'm not sure. I think that's the first time I heard it or I forgot it and that's beautiful, man. Yeah.

Probably, actually, that's sort of what we always come back to when we're having trouble making decisions or trying to finish a record, is just going on instinct and heart, because, as we've discussed today, things can get a bit cerebral. So, I think...

Just bring you back to the joy and the fun.

Yeah, and I think Tony is especially good at that, because we're trying to select songs to go on an album, how to make it flow and everything. He's sort of very good at just going, that doesn't feel right, that doesn't feel right, that doesn't feel right. And because we're so close, we can be so honest with each other. He can...

Often you're the one that will say that's just too...

Weird.

Yeah, weird or intellectual or...

Yeah, or whatever it is and bringing it back to the feeling and what what feels right.

Yeah.

Yeah.

Well, congratulations on the album. I was lucky enough to have a few listens over the weekend and yeah, it's really awesome.

Oh, thank you.

Kind of, yeah it reminds me of Wildflower a bit, that sort of energy but yeah.

Oh, great.

Really loved it.

A little bit...

Sorry.

It's alright.

You sure?

I was going to say it's a little bit rambunctious but is that a word?

It's a word.

Oh!

[Unclear audio at 00:29:14–00:29:20]

That's incredible.

It's going on the press release.

Thank you so much for joining me on the show today.

Thank you, [Unclear audio at 00:29:25–00:29:26].

Thank you.

A very big thank you again to the Avalanches for a very fun chat and you're about to hear for the very first time the band have kindly gifted us a sneaky little premiere for Triple R listeners of an unreleased Avalanches track from No Bad Memories that appears on the vinyl exclusive that is out tomorrow. This one features UK producer Vegyn. It's called Evergreen Altar.
